style_when: the story is a product, a device, a price or a market for a thing the reader could buy — an appliance, a panel, a router, a robot arm
prompt: On a brushed-steel workbench in a machine shop, an unbranded thin 16-inch laptop sits half-open at three-quarter angle, its display reflecting a single softbox key light from the left. To its right, five bare DDR5 memory modules are stacked as ascending steps, like a price ladder. Long contact shadows stretch right across graphite and slate grey steel, with one safety-yellow PCB edge accent. 85mm lens, shallow depth of field, fine film grain, asymmetric composition hero off-centre left and negative space right.
negative_prompt: garbled text, random lettering, watermarks, legible numbers, UI, logos
rationale: The story is about a purchasable laptop and its memory bill, so a studio product shot keeps the hero object tangible and legible. A single directional light and raised memory-rung stack communicate the price-ladder mechanism without generic datacenter imagery.
subject: unbranded thin laptop with half-raised display beside a stepped row of DDR5 memory modules as price-ladder rungs on a brushed-steel workbench
core_thesis: Nvidia's laptop launch is two ladders stacked: below 48GB the chip is cut, and above it the price is a memory purchase against an index that rose 13.3% in thirty days.
core_conflict: Fixed silicon decision at purchase versus daily-quoted DDR5 commodity memory price, with the entry chip rung cut and the top rung a $2,319 memory bill.
composition: asymmetric composition with hero laptop off-centre left, memory-rung stack rising toward upper-right, generous negative space right

review.depicts: An unbranded silver laptop with its display raised at a partial angle sits on a scratched brushed-metal workbench, with four upright DDR5 memory modules arranged in a stepped row to the right of the keyboard and blurred industrial machinery in the background.
review.reason: The frame shows the article's own two objects and mechanism — the laptop whose configuration is being priced and the memory modules standing as the ladder rungs of the memory-cost index — so a reader would recognise the subject of the headline.
